Vignette:
# Ama's Story

Ama was sixty-eight when she finally called the therapist's office, her voice steady but her hands trembling as she held the phone. She had been married to Samuel for forty-three years, and it was Samuel who had suggested she seek help. He had noticed her pacing at three in the morning, noticed the way she flinched when he moved too quickly, noticed that she no longer sat with him in the living room after dark. What he did not fully understand—what Ama herself was only beginning to name—was that the man who had hurt her so badly had died seventeen years ago, and yet his presence had somehow outlived him.

It happened on an evening in late spring, 2007. Ama's first husband, Kofi, had come home from work in a rage over something trivial—a bill, a comment she had made weeks earlier that he had been turning over in his mind. He had backed her into the kitchen, and when she tried to move past him, he had grabbed her by the throat and thrown her against the counter. She fell, and he kicked her twice in the ribs before she managed to crawl away and lock herself in the bedroom. The bruises had faded within weeks. The fear had not.

For years after Kofi's death in a car accident, Ama had felt almost normal. She had remarried Samuel, a gentle man who had never raised his voice to her. But somewhere around her sixty-fifth birthday, the memories had begun to surface with a force that startled her. They came without warning—a smell of soil from the garden, the particular way a man's voice deepened when he was tired, even the sensation of lying down to sleep—and suddenly she was back in that kitchen, her body braced for impact.

What frightened Ama most was the unpredictability of these intrusions. She would be folding laundry, and the memory would force its way in: not just the image of Kofi's face, but the exact pressure of his hand around her neck, the sound of her own breathing cut short. She had come to believe that if she could just keep the memory at bay long enough, she might be able to control when it emerged. So she had developed a habit of pushing it away the moment she felt it beginning, clamping down on the thought before it could fully take shape. But the cost of this vigilance was exhaustion.

Sleep had become nearly impossible. Ama would lie in bed beside Samuel and feel her body tense, her mind refusing to surrender to rest. To fall asleep meant to be vulnerable, to be unable to sense danger approaching. She had taken to staying awake until Samuel was deeply asleep, then sometimes sleeping in the guest room—but only if she positioned herself so that she could see the doorway. Sleeping alone in an unfamiliar place, such as when Samuel's sister invited them to visit, triggered a panic so acute that Ama had learned to decline invitations. She had come to believe that she could only truly be safe in her own bedroom, with the door locked and Samuel within earshot.

To manage the anxiety that now lived in her chest constantly, Ama had filled her days with activity. She volunteered at the church four days a week, organized the neighborhood book club, took on projects around the house that Samuel had been meaning to do for years. As long as her mind was occupied with tasks and other people's needs, she could keep the intrusive memories at a distance. She had become expert at reading what others wanted from her and providing it before they had to ask—if she could make people comfortable, she reasoned, perhaps they would not hurt her. Samuel had noticed that she seemed anxious to please him in ways she never had before, that she seemed unable to relax even when he explicitly told her he wanted nothing from her.

The real consequence had come when Samuel's daughter asked if Ama would help care for her newborn grandson while she returned to work. Ama had said yes immediately, before she could think. But the reality of being alone with the infant, of being responsible for another vulnerable person while her own sense of safety was so precarious, had sent her into a state of constant dread. She had called in sick after two weeks, then had not answered her daughter-in-law's calls. The shame of this failure had compounded her isolation.

It was Samuel who had finally said, gently, that he thought she needed to talk to someone. That perhaps the past was not as far behind her as she had believed. Ama had resisted at first, but the uncontrolled way the memories were beginning to surface, the way her vigilance was now affecting not just her sleep but her relationships, had worn her down. She was exhausted from the constant effort of staying busy, of staying alert, of keeping the memory just barely at arm's length. What she hoped for, sitting in the therapist's office for the first time, was simply to feel safe again—not just in her home, but in her own mind.
